report:
Conclusion: The checkpoints differ in a shallow, lexical/topic bias concentrated at the start of the sequence (the prefix). Model B’s residual-stream difference (B minus A) at early token positions in late layers pushes logits toward sensational / tabloidy / emotionally charged / explicit vocabulary.

Why I believe this
- Location and magnitude: the L2-norm of the difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at the earliest token positions (pos0, and to a lesser extent pos1–4), and in deep layers (layers ~11–25). That pattern indicates a change to the model’s prior or lexical preferences for sequence-start tokens rather than a distributed syntactic change later in generation.
- Logit-lens evidence: the top tokens that the difference vectors point to are dominated by tabloidy media names and sensational words (TMZ, DJI), marketing/scammer/business terms (marketers, scammers, payouts), violent/negative words (cannibal, deadly, graves, destruction, rifles, hated, hate), sexual/explicit tokens and adult-brand tokens (Playboy, herpes, fucking, homosexual), and emotionally salient adjectives (terrifying, genuinely, terrifying). Many cells also point to short heading-like tokens (Summary, Outcome, File, Waiter, plaintext), suggesting a bias toward label/heading starts in some contexts. This mix is consistent with a shift in topical/tonal priors toward gossipy, sensational, or explicit content at the start of text.
- Patchscope: no clear continuations were provided to contradict this; the decisive signal comes from the logit-lens/top-token directions and the prefix-concentrated norms.

I do not claim a specific training objective change (e.g., "was fine-tuned on tabloids") because the evidence only supports naming a lexical/topic bias at sequence start, not the exact cause.
